channel.title: Money Matters Daily — Pinterest Feed (Investing Basics)
channel.description: Curated, approved pins for the "Investing Basics" board. Not the main site feed.

item.title: ETFs vs. Mutual Funds: What's the Difference?
item.description: ETFs and mutual funds both pool money into a basket of investments, but they're bought, priced, and taxed differently. Here's how each one works, what the differences cost you, and how to decide which fits your situation.

item.title: What Is Cryptocurrency? How It Works and the Risks
item.description: Cryptocurrency is digital money recorded on a public ledger instead of a bank's books. Here's how it works in plain language, why it carries real risks, and what to check before you put any money near it.

item.title: Stock Market Indices Explained: S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq
item.description: The S&P 500, Dow, and Nasdaq show up in every market headline, but they measure different things in different ways. Here's what each one tracks, how weighting changes the result, why you can't buy an index directly, and how to read the numbers without being misled.

item.title: Japan's NISA Program Explained: Tax-Free Investing Basics
item.description: NISA lets investors in Japan keep all investment gains free of tax, permanently. Here's how the two account types work, the actual limits, and what changed for 2026.

item.title: How Superannuation Works: Australia's Retirement Savings Explained
item.description: Superannuation is compulsory, employer-funded retirement savings — currently 12% of your wages, locked away and invested until you're 60. Here's the actual mechanics.

item.title: TFSA vs. RRSP: Canada's Tax-Advantaged Accounts Explained
item.description: TFSAs and RRSPs both shelter your money from tax, but on opposite ends of the timeline. Here's how the 2026 contribution limits work, which one to prioritize, and why most people eventually need both.

item.title: Compound Interest Explained Simply
item.description: Compound interest is interest earned on interest, not just on what you put in — and the gap between simple and compound growth is small at first, then isn't. Here's the actual math.

item.title: How to Start Investing With Little Money
item.description: You don't need $1,000 to start investing — fractional shares and low/no-minimum brokers mean $20 a paycheck is enough to begin. Here's the actual order of operations.

item.title: Index Funds Explained for Beginners
item.description: You don't need to pick winning stocks — you need to own the market and let time compound. Here's what an index fund actually is and why it's usually the right default.
